extraction.pages_processed: 1-7 and 20-22 read in full; 8-19 read and keyword-screened; 23-29 endnotes not extracted
extraction.notes: Read in full: pages 1-7 (overview, methodology, sections I and II) and 20-22 (section VII). Pages 8-19 (sections III to VI: blocking and content removal, online media and the information environment, legal framework for rights online, arrests and harassment) were read and keyword-screened (digit*, electronic, cyber*, personal data, data protection, interoperab*, eID, 5G, broadband, ANRCETI, roaming, artificial intelligence, AI, platform, portal, signature, telecom*, infrastructure, privacy) and hold no in-scope claim. Pages 23-29 are endnotes and were not extracted. Text-file page numbers are printed page numbers plus one. Document check: the file is the Freedom House country report 'Internet Freedom in Moldova', dated October 2024 on its cover (the register gives 2024-11 and the title 'Freedom on the Net 2024: Moldova'). Its methodology note says it uses a modified Freedom on the Net 2024 methodology and that 'there are no scores associated with this report', so no FOTN numerical scores exist to extract; the register's coverage period (June 2023 to May 2024) is not printed and some events run to October 2024. The report states it does not reflect conditions in Transnistria (LIM-0044); no item concerns the region. Dates are from the register as instructed. Speaker is Freedom House unless a sentence attributes data to another body (ITU, ANRCETI, Speedtest, Cable, the two regulators, STISC, the Digital Quality of Life Index), then flagged reported_view. Left out under the rules: website blocking, emergency-powers blocking and content removal (section III), including the 2024 cybercrime law amendments on blocking orders; disinformation and AI deepfakes in disinformation campaigns, online media, news consumption (including the E-Governance Agency survey on news sources) and online organising (IV); freedom of expression, access to information and speech offences (V); arrests and harassment, including cyberattacks and DDoS against journalists and media outlets (VI, VII.4); anonymity, encryption and website-owner or SIM registration (VII.1); individual surveillance cases and criminal cases on illegal wiretapping and private surveillance (VII.2), the Moldova-Leaks hacking of officials' Telegram accounts and its criminal investigation (VII.4) as cybercrime enforcement; providers' cybercrime oversight obligations (II.1); internet shutdowns of 2009, the Moldtelecom gateway monopoly to 2010 and the 3G and 4G roll-out dates (before the window); Moldtelecom corruption and audit, telecom share of GDP, operators' revenue and market shares, the Orange-Sun Communications takeover (company economics, not access); constitutional background articles; ANRCETI's website publishing drafts (incidental). Doubtful for the analyst (theme_doubtful, 17 items): the surveillance, interception and data retention items in VII.2 and VII.3 tagged TECH-DATA (whether state surveillance law belongs to data governance); internet-use demographics (TECH-INFRA); Moldtelecom reorganisation; the Law on Information Society Services as TECH-DIGI; Cybercor's research and education tasks. Second-pass check (PC-05) by checker-CSO8 on 5 November 2026: 6 items added (review/RUN-2026-02/second_pass/MDA-CSO-2024-001.csv).

items.stated_text: The Law on Preventing and Combating Cybercrime obliges service providers to maintain records of service users and provide competent authorities with user data based on legal requests.

location.section: VII.3 Data Protection, Retention, and Access

items.intervention_as_stated: Law on Preventing and Combating Cybercrime (user records and data access)
items.extraction_note: theme_doubtful: a data retention and access obligation under the cybercrime law; tagged TECH-DATA for retention of personal data, though cybercrime enforcement is out of scope (rules section 4). Analyst to confirm.

pass2.classification_note: Theme doubtful resolved: data retention and access obligations under the cybercrime law; cybercrime enforcement is outside the theme (alpha ruling).

items.stated_text: Providers are required to monitor, supervise and store data to identify service providers, service users and channels through which messages are transmitted for 180 days. They must also comply with authorities’ requests to immediately store data when there is a risk of destruction or damage for no more than 120 days. Providers are also obliged to ensure that computer data contained in network protocol packets is decrypted and that the data is retained for 90 days.
items.summary: Providers must store identifying data for 180 days, preserve data on request up to 120 days, and decrypt and keep packet data 90 days.

location.section: VII.3 Data Protection, Retention, and Access

items.extraction_note: Same theme doubt as the previous item: retention obligations under the cybercrime law.

pass2.classification_note: Theme doubtful resolved: data retention and access obligations under the cybercrime law; cybercrime enforcement is outside the theme (alpha ruling).
